question: Which of the following regional map locations is NOT correctly associated with the loss of a major Dutch commercial monopoly or territory? [Monopoly Maps]
options: Ceylon (Sri Lanka) - Loss of the wild cinnamon monopoly to the British forces in 1796
Banda Islands (Indonesia) - Loss of the exclusive nutmeg monopoly after French spice-hunter Pierre Poivre smuggled nutmeg trees to Mauritius
Malabar Coast (India) - Loss of the black pepper monopoly following the Treaty of Mavelikkara with Travancore and British competition
Surat (Gujarat) - Loss of the saffron monopoly after Mughal forces seized the Dutch saffron plantations in Kashmir
wrong_fact: The Dutch never had a saffron monopoly, nor did they own saffron plantations in Kashmir. Surat was a trade depot for textiles, indigo, and spices, but saffron was not a Dutch-monopolized trade product in India.
explanation: Saffron trade was not a major concern of the Dutch East India Company, and they had no plantations in Kashmir (which was far inland and out of their reach). The other statements describe genuine losses of Dutch monopolies: the Ceylon cinnamon monopoly was lost to the British in 1795-96; the Banda nutmeg monopoly was broken in the 1770s when the French botanist Pierre Poivre smuggled nutmeg and clove plants to Mauritius and Reunion, ending the Dutch global monopoly; and the Malabar pepper monopoly collapsed due to Travancore's ascendance and British smuggling networks.

question: The gradual erosion of the Dutch trade network in the Indian Ocean can be mapped through the decline of its key factories. Which of the following statements regarding the loss of these posts is NOT correct? [Loss of Trade Posts]
options: Balasore (Odisha) - A Dutch factory established for textiles and saltpetre that was abandoned in the late 18th century due to the silting of the river and British competition in Bengal
Tuticorin (Gulf of Mannar) - The center of the Dutch pearl fishery and chank trade, which was seized by the British in 1781 during the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War
Patna (Bihar) - The crucial inland Dutch factory for saltpetre and opium procurement, which was occupied by the British in 1781 and never returned to operational independence
Diego Garcia (Chagos Archipelago) - A major Dutch naval refueling station that was ceded to the French in 1715 in exchange for Pondicherry
wrong_fact: Diego Garcia was never a major Dutch naval refueling station, nor was it traded for Pondicherry. Pondicherry was captured by the Dutch in 1693 and returned to the French under the Treaty of Ryswick (1697) in exchange for commercial concessions, not islands in the Chagos Archipelago.
explanation: Diego Garcia was explored by the Portuguese and later claimed by the French in the late 18th century, eventually falling to the British. It was never a Dutch naval base. The other factories mentioned represent actual Dutch inland and coastal losses: Balasore in Odisha declined due to geographical silting of the river and British dominance; Tuticorin's valuable pearl and shell fisheries were repeatedly seized by the British; and the Patna factory, which allowed the VOC direct access to Gangetic saltpetre and opium, was occupied by the British during global conflicts.

question: Which of the following statements correctly maps the final territorial liquidation of the Dutch East India Company's possessions on the Indian mainland under the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824? [Territorial Liquidation Map]
options: The treaty permanently exchanged all Dutch factories in India (including Chinsurah, Surat, and Negapatam) and Malacca for British cessions in Sumatra (Bencoolen)
The treaty allowed the Dutch to retain their factories in Malabar (Cochin) as sovereign enclaves, while ceding their Bengal factories to the British
Under the treaty, the Dutch ceded Trincomalee in Ceylon to the British in exchange for Singapore, which was then occupied by the VOC
The treaty drew a straight maritime boundary along the 10th parallel north, allocating all lands north of it (including Sumatra) to the British
wrong_fact: The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 did not allow the Dutch to retain Cochin or any other factories in India; it marked the complete and final exit of the Dutch from the Indian mainland and the Malay Peninsula, ceding all Indian posts and Malacca to the British in exchange for British cessions in Sumatra and the recognition of Sumatra/Indonesia as a Dutch sphere of influence.
explanation: The Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 (also known as the Treaty of London) finalized the division of spheres of influence in Southeast Asia and India. The Dutch gave up all factories in India (Chinsurah, Surat, Calicut, Negapatam, etc.) and Malacca. In return, the British ceded Bencoolen (Bengkulu) in Sumatra to the Dutch and withdrew their objections to Dutch dominance in Sumatra. This created a clear geographical line: the British dominated India and Malaya, while the Dutch dominated Indonesia. Ceylon had already been ceded in 1802.
